title: Projection bodies and products of simplices
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: OpenAI's product counterexample (2026) to the simplex maximum for projection-body volume: the affine invariant R_d(K) = |Pi K|/|K|^(d-1) of T_10 x T_10 exceeds the simplex value c_20 by the factor 22,355,476/22,020,096, and products of simplices exceed c_n by an exponential factor lambda^n in all large dimensions. The course proves Cauchy's formula for the projection body of a polytope (a zonotope of facet vectors), affine covariance, the extension to convex bodies by circumscribed polytopes, and multiplicativity on products; computes the simplex value c_d = (d+1) d^d/d! from a cube plus one diagonal segment; and shows that dimension twenty is the first in which a product of simplices exceeds the simplex value.
prerequisites: Lebesgue measure: core course Measure and Integration (Fremlin, Measure Theory, Volumes 1 and 2): translation invariance (134A), Lebesgue measure on R^(r+s) as a product measure (251N), Fubini's theorem (252B), linear maps (263A)
compactness in R^d and the extreme value theorem: core course Real Analysis II (Lebl, Basic Analysis, Theorem 7.5.6)

checks.reading: The manuscript 'A product counterexample to the simplex maximum for projection-body volume' (OpenAI, 24 Sep 2026; build/main.tex and references.tex, 487 + 48 lines, 21 kB of TeX; local library copy openai-math-20261006) was read in full on 17 Oct 2026, and every step was derived again while the lessons were written. No error was found. Changes of form in the course: (1) polytopes are taken as bounded intersections of finitely many half-spaces with no superfluous inequality, so facets and products of polytopes are described directly; the almost-everywhere count of the two facets over a point of the shadow is written out; (2) the extension to convex bodies uses circumscribed polytopes cut out by supporting half-spaces in finitely many directions, where the manuscript uses inscribed convex hulls of finite nets (which would need the equivalence of the two descriptions of polytopes); (3) Proposition 2.2 of the third lesson adds that no product of simplices of dimensions at least two exceeds the simplex value below dimension twenty (exact evaluation of the 72 pairs and an induction on the number of factors); (4) the zonotope volume formula is proved as an exercise from the extrusion lemma. Context checked: Feng, Hu, Liu and Xu (preprint, MathSciDoc 2608.23002; Theorem 1.3: counterexamples in every dimension d >= 9 with at most d + 2 facets; Section 1 for Brannen's bound and its validity in dimensions two and three); Chen, Feng, Li, Xi and Xu (preprint, MathSciDoc 2608.23001, Theorem 1.2: R_3 <= 18, attained by tetrahedra). Brannen's paper (Mathematika 1996) and Petty's 1967 note are not freely accessible; the course attributes the conjecture through [FHLX].
checks.exact_checks: Python with fractions, numpy and scipy (plan/checks_20261017/projection_body_check.py, output projection_body_check.out, 17 Oct 2026): 476 checks, 0 problems. Cauchy's facet formula against direct projection volumes of random polytopes in R^3 and R^4 (floating point); the sum of facet vectors is zero; the zonotope volume formula against convex hulls; the support function of Pi(A x B) and R_4(A x B) = R_2(A) R_2(B) for random polygons; |T_d| and the facet vectors of T_3, T_4; |[0,1]^d + [0,w]| = d + 1 and R_d(T_d) = c_d exactly for d <= 10; the ratio 22,355,476/22,020,096 and the integer certificate 335,380; the product test formula for r, s <= 15; rho < 1 for all 72 pairs with r + s <= 19 and the table of the third lesson; the first dimension 20 over all products of simplices; c_10, A = c_10/beta^10 and c_n < (n+1) beta^n for n < 60; a threshold N = 47 for lambda = (1 + A^(1/10))/2 in floating-point logarithms.
